questions.q: A Generalized Sequential Machine (GSM) is formally defined as a tuple with how many components?
questions.e: A GSM is a six-tuple M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, λ): states, input alphabet, output alphabet, transition function, initial state, and output function.

questions.q: In a GSM M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, λ), what is the type (signature) of the output function λ?
questions.e: In a GSM the output function is λ : Q × Σ → Γ*, so each state/input pair emits a (possibly empty or multi-symbol) output word over Γ.

questions.q: A GSM is called a Mealy machine exactly when which condition holds for every state q and input symbol a?
questions.e: A Mealy machine is the special GSM whose output on every transition is exactly one symbol, i.e. |λ(q,a)| = 1 for all q and a.

questions.q: In a Moore machine M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, λ, q0), the output symbol produced depends on:
o: the current state and the input symbol
questions.e: A Moore machine's output function is λ : Q → Γ, so output is determined solely by the state the machine is in, independent of the input read.

questions.q: For a GSM M, the transition graph labels an arrow from p to q with 'a/w' to indicate:
o: p accepts a and rejects w
the stack pushes w on input a
questions.e: The label a/w on the edge p → q means the machine reads input a moving to state q (δ(p,a)=q) while outputting the word w (λ(p,a)=w).

questions.q: Every GSM M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, λ) has an associated DFA. What is the final-state set of that corresponding DFA?
questions.e: The DFA corresponding to a GSM is (Q, Σ, δ, q0, ∅) — it has an empty set of accepting states, since a GSM's job is producing output, not accepting.

questions.q: When converting a Moore machine to an equivalent Mealy machine, how is the Mealy output function λ' defined?
questions.e: In Moore-to-Mealy conversion the states, transitions and start state are kept identical, and the Mealy output on a transition is the Moore output of the destination state: λ'(q,σ) = λ(δ(q,σ)).

questions.q: When a Moore machine is translated into an equivalent Mealy machine, its set of states is:
questions.e: Moore-to-Mealy translation uses Q' = Q, δ' = δ and q0' = q0; only the placement of the output changes, so the state set stays the same.

questions.q: In converting a Mealy machine to an equivalent Moore machine, the new states take the form:
o: pairs (q, o) of a state and an output symbol
questions.e: Mealy-to-Moore conversion splits states by output: Q' = {(q,o) | q ∈ Q, o an output of q}, so each new state is a pair of an original state and an output symbol o, with λ'((q,o)) = o.

questions.q: If G : Σ* → Γ* is a GSM-computable function and L ⊆ Σ* is regular, then the image G(L) is:
questions.e: Regular languages are closed under GSM-computable functions: for regular L, G(L) = {G(v) | v ∈ L} is regular, and for regular K the preimage G⁻¹(K) is also regular.

questions.q: A word function of the form G : Σ* → Γ* is used to model:
questions.e: A formal language models a decision problem (Σ* → {yes,no}); by contrast a word function G : Σ* → Γ* models problems whose output is itself a word, e.g. counting or transduction tasks.

questions.q: A single-state GSM suffices to compute which of the following transductions?
o: Morse-code encoding of letters and digits
questions.e: Morse coding assigns a fixed dot/dash code to each symbol independently, so a one-state GSM that outputs each letter's code realises the encoding word function.

questions.q: A GSM that reads a base-4 digit string and outputs pairs of bits (0→00, 1→01, 2→10, 3→11) computes:
o: the binary representation of the number
questions.e: Interpreting the input as a base-4 numeral and mapping each digit to its two-bit code yields the binary representation; e.g. input 311 (=53) gives output 110101.

questions.q: A decision problem is modelled by a formal language as a map of which form?
questions.e: Decision problems have yes/no answers, so they are modelled by FL : Σ* → {yes, no}, where the language collects exactly the inputs whose answer is 'yes'.

questions.q: In the proof that regular languages are closed under a (Mealy) GSM-computable function, the new automaton B is built using which construction?
o: a product construction on Q × Q'
questions.e: The proof forms an NFA B on the product state set P = Q × Q', combining the DFA for L with the GSM, so that L(B) = G(L).

questions.q: For a run ρ = (r0, a1, r1, …, an, rn) of a GSM M, the output word is:
questions.e: The output of a GSM along a run is the concatenation of the per-transition outputs λ(r0,a1)λ(r1,a2)…λ(r(n-1),an) ∈ Γ*.

questions.q: The primary motivation for constructing a minimal DFA is:
o: a space-efficient implementation of a regular language
questions.e: Minimization seeks a DFA with the fewest states recognising the same language, giving a space-efficient implementation of the regular language.

questions.q: Two states p and q of a DFA are defined to be equivalent when:
o: for every word w, δ*(p,w) is accepting iff δ*(q,w) is accepting
they have the same number of outgoing edges
questions.e: States p and q are equivalent iff for all w ∈ Σ*, δ*(p,w) ∈ F ⇔ δ*(q,w) ∈ F — no word distinguishes them by acceptance.

questions.q: In the marking algorithm, which pairs of states are marked first (by ε)?
o: pairs where one state is accepting and the other is not
questions.e: Step 1 marks every pair (p,q) with p ∈ F and q ∉ F (distinguished by the empty word ε), since an accepting and a non-accepting state can never be equivalent.

questions.q: During refinement, an unmarked pair (p,q) becomes marked by 'av' precisely when:
o: (δ(p,a), δ(q,a)) is already marked by v
p and q are both final
questions.e: The inductive rule marks (p,q) by av whenever the pair of a-successors (δ(p,a), δ(q,a)) is already marked (distinguished) by some word v.

questions.q: A minimal DFA is unique in what sense?
questions.e: For any two DFAs accepting the same language, their minimal DFAs are isomorphic — identical up to the naming of states.

questions.q: In the equivalence matrix, why are the diagonal entries (qi, qi) omitted?
o: a state is always equivalent to itself
questions.e: Every state is trivially equivalent to itself, so the diagonal entries (qi, qi) carry no information and are not filled in.

questions.q: Why does the equivalence matrix only fill entries (qi, qj) with i < j?
o: to save marks for final states
questions.e: Equivalence is symmetric, so (qi, qj) and (qj, qi) hold the same information; only one half of the matrix (i < j) needs to be computed.

questions.q: States p and q are inequivalent (distinguishable) exactly when:
o: there is a word w with δ*(p,w) ∈ F and δ*(q,w) ∉ F (or vice versa)
questions.e: p and q are inequivalent iff some word w takes one to an accepting state and the other to a non-accepting state — that w distinguishes them.

questions.q: After minimization by merging equivalent states, what is the relationship between L(M) and L(Mmin)?
o: L(Mmin) is the complement of L(M)
questions.e: Merging equivalent states preserves the language: for every DFA M, L(M) = L(Mmin).

questions.q: When the refinement (marking) procedure is applied, the algorithm stops when:
o: no further pairs get newly marked in a full pass
questions.e: The marking is repeated until a complete pass produces no change; the remaining unmarked pairs are the equivalent state pairs.

questions.q: At termination of the algorithm, the pairs of states that remain UNMARKED are exactly the:
questions.e: Marking records distinguishability; a pair left unmarked cannot be distinguished by any word, so unmarked pairs are precisely the equivalent (mergeable) states.

questions.q: A context-free grammar is formally a quadruple G = (N, Σ, P, S). Which component is the start symbol?
questions.e: In G = (N, Σ, P, S), N is the nonterminals, Σ the terminals, P the productions, and S ∈ N is the designated start symbol.

questions.q: In a context-free grammar, every production rule must have the form:
o: A → aB or A → a only
α → β with α, β arbitrary strings
A → α with A a single nonterminal and α ∈ (N ∪ Σ)*
β1 A β2 → β1 α β2
questions.e: A CFG production is A → α where the left side A is a single nonterminal and the right side α is any string over N ∪ Σ. The 'context-free' name comes from replacing A regardless of surroundings.

questions.q: For a CFG G = (N, Σ, P, S), which condition on the alphabets always holds?
questions.e: The nonterminal and terminal alphabets are disjoint: N ∩ Σ = ∅.

questions.q: Which grammar generates the language {a^n b^n | n ≥ 0}?
questions.e: S → aSb | ε produces one a and one b per recursive step and terminates with ε, generating exactly {a^n b^n | n ≥ 0}.

questions.q: What is the relationship between the class of regular languages and the class of context-free languages?
o: CFLs are a proper subset of regular languages
regular languages are a proper subset of CFLs
questions.e: Every regular language is context-free, and some CFLs (e.g. {a^n b^n}) are not regular, so the regular languages form a proper subset of the CFLs.

questions.q: The language generated by a CFG G is defined as:
questions.e: L(G) = {w ∈ Σ* | S ⇒* w}: the terminal words derivable from the start symbol in finitely many steps.

questions.q: A context-free grammar G is called ambiguous if:
o: it has more than one nonterminal
some word in L(G) has more than one parse (derivation) tree
questions.e: Ambiguity is a property of the grammar: G is ambiguous when at least one word of L(G) can be generated by two or more distinct parse trees.

questions.q: A leftmost derivation is one in which, at each step:
questions.e: In a leftmost derivation the leftmost nonterminal of the current sentential form is the one rewritten at every step.

questions.q: Backus–Naur (BNF) rules are typically used to specify:
questions.e: BNF rules — a form of context-free grammar — are the classic way to define the syntax of programming-language constructs such as arithmetic expressions.

questions.q: In a derivation tree for a CFG, the sequence of leaf labels (read left to right) is:
questions.e: The root is the start symbol and the leaves are terminals; reading the leaves left to right yields the generated word.

questions.q: Two grammars G1 and G2 are said to be equivalent when:
o: they have the same start symbol
questions.e: Grammar equivalence is defined by the languages generated: G1 and G2 are equivalent iff L(G1) = L(G2), regardless of their rules.

questions.q: When a DFA M = (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F) is converted into an equivalent CFG, an accepting state q ∈ F contributes which production?
questions.e: For each final state q the construction adds q → ε; a transition δ(q,a)=q' adds q → aq'. Nonterminals are the states with q0 as start symbol.

questions.q: A sentential form γ is 'directly derivable' from β when γ is obtained from β by:
o: applying one production to a single nonterminal occurrence in β
questions.e: Direct derivation (β ⇒ γ) means β = δ1 A δ2 and γ = δ1 α δ2 for some production A → α — exactly one nonterminal is rewritten by one rule.

questions.q: A language L ⊆ Σ* is called a context-free language when:
o: it is accepted by a DFA
it is generated by some context-free grammar
questions.e: By definition L is context-free iff there exists a context-free grammar G with L(G) = L.

questions.q: In the standard naming conventions for grammars, terminals and nonterminals are distinguished by:
questions.e: By convention nonterminal symbols begin with uppercase letters and terminal symbols with lowercase letters; the start symbol is the LHS of the first production.

questions.q: A grammar is in Chomsky Normal Form when every production has one of which two forms?
o: β1 A β2 → β1 α β2
questions.e: Chomsky Normal Form allows only A → BC (two nonterminals) or A → a (a single terminal).

questions.q: A grammar is in Greibach Normal Form when every rule has the form:
questions.e: Greibach Normal Form requires each rule to begin with exactly one terminal followed by zero or more nonterminals: A → aB1…Bk, k ≥ 0.

questions.q: A right-linear grammar allows only rules of the form:
questions.e: Right-linear rules are A → aB or A → a, with a single terminal optionally followed by a single nonterminal on the right.

questions.q: In converting a grammar to CNF, the step that introduces a fresh nonterminal Ba with rule Ba → a is used to:
o: ensure terminals appear only in rules of the form A → a
questions.e: To make terminals appear only in A → a rules, each terminal a gets a nonterminal Ba (with Ba → a), and every occurrence of a inside longer rules is replaced by Ba.

questions.q: A 'chain rule' (unit rule) that must be eliminated during CNF conversion has the form:
questions.e: A unit/chain rule is one whose right side is a single nonterminal, A → B; these are removed by adding, for each such chain, the non-unit productions of the reached nonterminal.

questions.q: To eliminate a production A → A1 A2 … An with n > 2, the standard procedure:
o: introduces B, replacing it by A → A1 B and B → A2…An
questions.e: Long right sides are shortened iteratively: A → A1 A2…An (n>2) becomes A → A1 B together with a new rule B → A2…An, repeated until only two symbols remain.

questions.q: A 'null production' targeted for elimination in CNF conversion is a rule of the form:
questions.e: Null (ε) productions have the form A → ε; step 1 of CNF conversion eliminates them (using a fresh start symbol S' → S | ε to still allow the empty word).

questions.q: What is the exact relationship between right-linear grammars and Greibach Normal Form?
o: every right-linear grammar is in GNF, but not conversely
neither is contained in the other
questions.e: A right-linear rule A → aB (or A → a) already fits the GNF pattern A → aB1…Bk, so every right-linear grammar is in GNF; the converse fails because GNF allows several trailing nonterminals.

questions.q: Which statement about Chomsky Normal Form is correct?
o: only regular grammars have a CNF form
every context-free grammar has an equivalent CNF grammar
only some CFGs have an equivalent CNF grammar
questions.e: Every context-free grammar (handling ε separately) can be transformed into an equivalent grammar in Chomsky Normal Form.

questions.q: The preliminary 'Step 0' in CNF conversion, adding a new start symbol S' with rule S' → S, ensures that:
o: the start symbol never appears on the right-hand side of a rule
questions.e: Introducing S' → S guarantees the (new) start symbol does not occur on any right-hand side, which is needed so ε-handling and later steps behave correctly.

questions.q: When eliminating a null production A → ε, given another rule B → αAβ, the procedure adds which rule?
questions.e: Removing A → ε requires compensating by adding, for each occurrence of A, the version with A deleted: B → αAβ yields the added rule B → αβ.

questions.q: In Greibach Normal Form, every rule's right-hand side begins with:
questions.e: GNF rules A → aB1…Bk all start with a single terminal a, followed only by nonterminals.

questions.q: Establishing a normal form that guarantees each nonterminal produces at least one terminal symbol is important because it makes which problem decidable with finitely many cases to inspect?
questions.e: For the word problem (is w ∈ L(G)?), CNF ensures every derivation step makes measurable progress toward terminals, bounding the derivation length and leaving only finitely many combinations to check (as in CYK).

questions.q: In a CNF rule of the form A → BC, the symbols B and C must be:
questions.e: The binary CNF form A → BC requires both B and C to be nonterminals; terminals may appear only alone, as A → a.

questions.q: A right-linear grammar generates exactly which class of languages?
questions.e: Right-linear (type-3) grammars generate precisely the regular languages, and each corresponds directly to a finite automaton.

questions.q: Before running the CYK algorithm on a word, the grammar must first be transformed into:
questions.e: CYK operates on a grammar in Chomsky Normal Form (rules A → BC or A → a), which lets it fill its table by combining two shorter segments.

questions.q: In CYK, the base-case set N(i,i) for a single letter ai contains exactly those nonterminals A such that:
o: A ⇒* ai for some longer path
questions.e: For length-1 segments, N(i,i) = {A | A → ai ∈ P}: the nonterminals that directly produce the letter ai.

questions.q: For a segment w[i,j] with i < j, CYK computes N(i,j) by looking for rules A → BC with:
o: B ∈ N(i,k) and C ∈ N(k+1,j) for some split point k
B and C both in N(i,i)
questions.e: A nonterminal A covers w[i,j] if some split k gives B covering w[i,k] and C covering w[k+1,j], i.e. B ∈ N(i,k), C ∈ N(k+1,j), with A → BC ∈ P.

questions.q: The CYK algorithm accepts the word w = a1…an exactly when:
questions.e: w ∈ L(G) iff the start symbol appears in the top-level cell: S ∈ N(1,n).

questions.q: The set of context-free languages is closed under which operations?
questions.e: CFLs are closed under concatenation, union and iteration (Kleene star), but not under intersection or complement.

questions.q: The class of context-free languages is NOT closed under:
questions.e: CFLs fail to be closed under both intersection and complement, unlike the regular languages which are closed under all these operations.

questions.q: The emptiness problem for a CFG G (is L(G) = ∅?) is decided by checking whether:
o: the start symbol S is productive
questions.e: L(G) = ∅ iff the start symbol is not productive; the algorithm marks terminals productive and propagates, then answers based on whether S becomes productive.

questions.q: In the emptiness algorithm, a symbol is marked 'productive' when:
o: it appears on some left-hand side
it can derive a terminal word
questions.e: A symbol is productive if it can generate a terminal string; terminals start productive, and A becomes productive once some rule A → α has all of α productive.

questions.q: For context-free languages, which decision problem is UNDECIDABLE?
questions.e: For CFLs, membership and emptiness are decidable, but equivalence L1 = L2 is undecidable (in contrast to regular languages, where all three are decidable).

questions.q: For regular languages, the equivalence problem L1 = L2 is:
questions.e: Unlike CFLs, regular languages have a decidable equivalence problem, along with decidable membership and emptiness.

questions.q: To build a CFG for the union L1 ∪ L2 from grammars G1, G2 with fresh start S, one adds the rule(s):
questions.e: Union is obtained with S → S1 | S2 (choosing either grammar's start symbol), keeping the two rule sets disjoint.

questions.q: To build a CFG for the Kleene star L1* from grammar G1 with fresh start S, one adds:
questions.e: Iteration L1* is generated by S → ε | S1 S, allowing zero or more concatenated copies of L1.

questions.q: To build a CFG for the concatenation L1·L2, the fresh start symbol gets a rule of the form:
questions.e: Concatenation is obtained by S → S1 S2, deriving a word of L1 followed by a word of L2.

questions.q: The membership problem 'w ∈ L(G)?' for a context-free language is:
questions.e: Membership for CFLs is decidable; the CYK algorithm decides it in the ε-free case after conversion to CNF.

questions.q: CYK fills its table in a dynamic-programming manner over segments of the input arranged as:
o: an upper-triangular matrix indexed by (i,j) with i ≤ j
questions.e: CYK considers segments w[i,j] of increasing length, storing N(i,j) in the upper-triangular part of an n×n matrix (entries with i > j are unused).

questions.q: A pushdown automaton extends a finite automaton with what kind of memory?
questions.e: A PDA adds an unbounded stack to a finite automaton; only the top (most recently pushed) symbol is accessible at any time.

questions.q: A pushdown automaton is formally defined as a tuple with how many components?
questions.e: A PDA is a 7-tuple A = (Q, Σ, Γ, ∆, q0, Z0, F): states, input alphabet, stack alphabet, transition relation, initial state, initial stack symbol, and final states.

questions.q: In the PDA tuple (Q, Σ, Γ, ∆, q0, Z0, F), the symbol Γ denotes the:
questions.e: Γ is the stack alphabet — the set of symbols that may appear on the PDA's stack. Σ is the (separate) input alphabet.

questions.q: In the PDA tuple, Z0 is the:
questions.e: Z0 ∈ Γ is the initial stack symbol, present on the stack at the start of every computation.

questions.q: The transition relation of a PDA has which form?
questions.e: A PDA's transition relation is ∆ ⊆ Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) × Γ × Q × Γ*: from a state, optionally reading input and popping a stack symbol, it moves to a new state pushing a string of stack symbols.

questions.q: The effect of applying a transition (p, a, Z, q, γ) is to:
o: pop Z, move to q, push the string γ, and advance past input a
push Z and read γ from input
stay in p and read a
questions.e: In state p reading a with Z on top, the PDA pops Z, transitions to q, pushes γ (first symbol of γ ending on top), and moves to the next input symbol.

questions.q: A configuration of a PDA is a triple (q, γ, w) representing:
o: state, stack contents, and remaining input
questions.e: A PDA configuration is (q, γ, w) ∈ Q × Γ* × Σ*: the current state q, the stack contents γ, and the unread rest w of the input word.

questions.q: Standard PDAs are:
questions.e: PDAs are nondeterministic and permit ε-transitions (moves that manipulate the stack without reading input).

questions.q: By acceptance with final states, a PDA accepts w when a run from (q0, Z0, w) reaches a configuration:
questions.e: Acceptance by final state means the input is fully consumed and the machine is in an accepting state: the run ends at (q, γ, ε) with q ∈ F.

questions.q: For acceptance 'by empty stack', a run (κ0,…,κn) is accepting when the final configuration is:
o: (q, ε, ε) for any q ∈ Q
questions.e: Empty-stack acceptance requires the run to end at (q, ε, ε) — the whole input read and the stack emptied — and no final states are needed.

questions.q: What is the relationship between acceptance by final state and acceptance by empty stack for PDAs?
o: only empty-stack PDAs can be nondeterministic
final-state PDAs are strictly more powerful
they recognise exactly the same class of languages
empty-stack PDAs are strictly more powerful
questions.e: A language is PDA-recognisable by final state iff it is recognisable by a PDA accepting with empty stack — the two acceptance modes have equal power.

questions.q: A cited motivation for the PDA's stack is that it can abstractly model:
o: the call stack of a recursive program
questions.e: The LIFO stack naturally models the call stack of recursive procedures, which is the intuitive motivation given for pushdown storage.

questions.q: A standard PDA for {a^n b^n | n ≥ 0} operates by:
o: pushing a counter symbol for each a and popping one for each b
questions.e: The PDA pushes a marker (e.g. Z) for each a read, then pops one marker for each b; accepting when the stack returns to empty ensures equal counts.

questions.q: In the graphical representation of a PDA, an edge is labelled with a triple of the form:
o: (σ, Z, γ) — input symbol, popped stack symbol, pushed string
questions.e: An edge from p to q labelled σ, Z, γ encodes the transition (p, σ, Z, q, γ): read σ (or ε), pop Z, push γ.

questions.q: Once a PDA reaches a configuration with an empty stack, it:
o: can no longer perform any transition
questions.e: With an empty stack there is no top symbol to pop, so no transition applies; such a configuration can only be the last one in a run.

questions.q: If a PDA's memory were reorganised so new symbols are appended at the end and read from the front, the resulting model is a:
questions.e: That FIFO variant is a queue system (queue automaton); allowing memory access at any position instead gives a Turing machine.

questions.q: The equivalence theorem for pushdown automata states that a language is PDA-recognisable if and only if it is:
questions.e: A language is recognised by some PDA exactly when it is context-free — PDAs characterise the context-free languages.

questions.q: In the construction of a PDA from a grammar in Chomsky Normal Form, how many states does the PDA use?
questions.e: The grammar-to-PDA construction uses a single state q0 (accepting by empty stack); all the work is done on the stack.

questions.q: In converting a CNF grammar to a PDA, the stack alphabet Γ is taken to be:
questions.e: The construction sets Γ := N: nonterminals of the grammar are used as the stack symbols, with the start symbol S as the initial stack symbol.

questions.q: A grammar rule A → BC (in CNF) becomes which PDA transition?
questions.e: A rule A → BC yields the ε-transition (q0, ε, A, q0, BC): pop A and push BC without reading input.

questions.q: A grammar rule A → a (in CNF) becomes which PDA transition?
questions.e: A rule A → a yields (q0, a, A, q0, ε): read the terminal a while popping A (pushing nothing).

questions.q: In the grammar-to-PDA construction, the initial stack symbol Z0 is set to:
questions.e: The stack starts with the grammar's start symbol: Z0 = S, and acceptance is by empty stack.

questions.q: When converting a PDA to an equivalent grammar, the nonterminals are chosen to be:
o: triples of the form [pZq] plus a start symbol S
questions.e: The PDA-to-grammar construction uses nonterminals [pZq] (meaning: from state p with Z on top, empty Z reaching q) together with a start symbol S and rules S → [q0 Z0 q].

questions.q: A deterministic pushdown automaton (DPDA) is one in which:
o: at most one transition is applicable in every configuration
questions.e: A PDA is deterministic if in every configuration at most one transition can be applied (with the usual condition preventing a conflicting ε-move).

questions.q: Is every regular language DPDA-recognisable?
o: yes — a DPDA can simulate any DFA without using the stack
only if the language is finite
no, DPDAs are weaker than DFAs
questions.e: Every DFA can be simulated by a DPDA that ignores its stack, so every regular language is DPDA-recognisable.

questions.q: Which statement about DPDAs and context-free languages is correct?
o: some CFLs are not DPDA-recognisable (e.g. palindromes over {a,b})
DPDAs recognise exactly the regular languages
questions.e: The DPDA-recognisable languages are a proper subclass of the CFLs; the palindrome language Lp over {a,b} is context-free but not DPDA-recognisable.

questions.q: The language {a^n b^n | n ≥ 0} is an example of a language that is:
o: recognisable only by a Turing machine
questions.e: {a^n b^n} is context-free and even deterministic (a DPDA recognises it), yet it is not regular — showing DPDA power strictly exceeds regularity.

questions.q: Why is the usual PDA for {a^n b^n | n ≥ 0} (with states q0, q1, q2) NOT deterministic?
o: two transitions are applicable in configuration (q0, Z0, a)
the stack alphabet is too small
questions.e: In the configuration (q0, Z0, a) both a push move and an ε-move to accept are possible, so more than one transition applies — violating determinism.

questions.q: A left derivation of a word in a grammar is one in which at each step:
questions.e: A left derivation always rewrites the leftmost nonterminal; the observation is that α ⇒ⁿ w iff α ⇒ⁿ w by a leftmost derivation.

questions.q: The corollary of the construction L(GA) = L(A) is that:
questions.e: Since a grammar GA can be built with L(GA) = L(A) for any empty-stack PDA A, every PDA-recognisable language is context-free.

questions.q: Every DPDA-recognisable language is necessarily:
questions.e: A DPDA is a special PDA, so every DPDA-recognisable language is PDA-recognisable and therefore context-free.

questions.q: According to the pumping lemma for regular languages, a sufficiently long word w ∈ L can be written as w = xyz with which properties?
o: x ≠ ε, |yz| ≤ n, and xyz^k ∈ L
y ≠ ε, |xy| ≤ n, and xy^k z ∈ L for all k
questions.e: The pumping lemma guarantees a split w = xyz with y ≠ ε, |xy| ≤ n, and xy^k z ∈ L for every k ∈ ℕ (the middle part can be repeated or deleted).

questions.q: The pumping lemma for regular languages is best described as:
o: a construction of the minimal DFA
a necessary condition for regularity, used to prove non-regularity
questions.e: It is a necessary (not sufficient) condition: every regular language satisfies it, so failing it proves a language is not regular.

questions.q: The core idea behind the pumping lemma's proof is that a long enough run:
o: must repeat a state (pigeonhole), creating a loop that can be repeated
questions.e: If a word is at least as long as the number of states, some state repeats in the accepting run (pigeonhole); the loop between the repeats is the pumpable part y.

questions.q: The language L = {w ∈ {0,1}* | |w|0 = |w|1} (equal numbers of 0s and 1s) is:
questions.e: This language is not regular: distinguishing it requires remembering the unbounded difference between counts of 0s and 1s, which finite memory cannot do.

questions.q: The language {w ∈ {0,1}* | |w|0 is divisible by 9} is:
questions.e: Only the count of 0s modulo 9 must be tracked, which needs just 9 states, so the language is regular.

questions.q: The language {w ∈ {0,1}* | |w|1 ≥ 4748} is:
o: regular (finitely many states counting up to 4748)
questions.e: One only needs to count 1s up to the threshold 4748 (4749 states), after which the answer is fixed — so the language is regular.

questions.q: To prove a language L is not regular using the pumping lemma, one must show that:
o: L has an even number of words
for the pumping length n, there is a word w ∈ L, |w| ≥ n, whose every valid split violates a pumping condition
questions.e: The proof exhibits a word w ∈ L with |w| ≥ n such that every decomposition w = xyz satisfying y ≠ ε and |xy| ≤ n produces some xy^k z ∉ L.

questions.q: In the pumping-lemma proof that {0^n 1^n} is not regular, choosing w = 0^n 1^n forces the pumped part y to consist of:
questions.e: Because |xy| ≤ n and the first n symbols are all 0s, x and y lie in the 0-block; pumping then changes the number of 0s, breaking the equality with the 1s.

questions.q: The condition on the middle part y in the pumping lemma is:
questions.e: The pumpable middle segment must be non-empty (y ≠ ε); otherwise repeating it would say nothing.

questions.q: The 'pump zero times' case of the lemma refers to the string:
questions.e: Setting k = 0 gives xy^0 z = xz, deleting the loop; the lemma guarantees this word is still in L.

questions.q: The language L = {ww | w ∈ {0,1}*} is:
questions.e: Recognising ww requires remembering the entire first half to compare with the second, which unbounded finite memory cannot do — it is not regular.

questions.q: The language of correctly balanced parentheses is:
questions.e: Balanced parentheses require tracking an unbounded count of open-but-unclosed brackets, so the language is not regular (though it is context-free).

questions.q: The mnemonic given for the weakness of finite automata says they cannot handle:
o: properties needing an unbounded counter, arbitrary-length pattern repetition, or arbitrary bracket depth
questions.e: Finite automata are too weak for: counting requiring an unbounded range, repetition of patterns of arbitrary length (like ww), and expressions of arbitrary bracket depth.

questions.q: Why are not all languages regular, as motivated before the pumping lemma?
o: all languages are in fact regular
there are more languages than regular expressions
questions.e: There are strictly more languages than there are regular expressions (a counting argument), so some languages cannot be regular.

questions.q: The number n whose existence the pumping lemma asserts (the pumping length) is related to:
o: the length of the shortest word
the number of states of an automaton for L
the number of final states only
questions.e: The pumping length can be taken as the number of states of an NFA for L; a word at least that long forces a repeated state.

questions.q: In the pumping lemma for context-free languages, a sufficiently long word z is decomposed into how many parts?
questions.e: The CFL pumping lemma splits z into five parts: z = uvwxy, and pumps the two parts v and x together.

questions.q: Condition (i) of the CFL pumping lemma requires that:
questions.e: The pumped parts together must be non-empty: vx ≠ ε (at least one of v, x is non-empty).

questions.q: Condition (ii) of the CFL pumping lemma bounds which substring's length by n?
questions.e: The middle block satisfies |vwx| ≤ n, restricting how far apart the two pumped segments can be.

questions.q: Condition (iii) of the CFL pumping lemma states that for all k ≥ 0:
o: u v^k w x^k y ∈ L
u^k v w x y^k ∈ L
questions.e: Both v and x are pumped simultaneously: u v^k w x^k y ∈ L for every k ≥ 0.

questions.q: The pumping lemma for CFLs is used to prove that a language is:
questions.e: As a necessary condition for context-freeness, its failure proves a language is not context-free.

questions.q: Which language is shown, via the CFL pumping lemma, to be NOT context-free?
questions.e: {a^n b^n c^n | n ≥ 0} is not context-free: |vwx| ≤ n confines vwx to at most two of the three letter blocks, so pumping unbalances the counts.

questions.q: The intuition behind the CFL pumping lemma is that a long word's derivation tree is so tall that:
o: the start symbol appears twice at the root
some nonterminal repeats along a single branch
questions.e: A sufficiently tall parse tree forces a nonterminal to repeat on one long branch; the subtree between the two occurrences yields the pumpable v and x.

questions.q: In proving {a^n b^n c^n} is not context-free, the bound |vwx| ≤ n implies vwx lies entirely within:
o: the prefix a^n b^n or the suffix b^n c^n (never spanning all three blocks)
questions.e: Since |vwx| ≤ n, the window vwx cannot cover parts of all three blocks; it fits inside a^n b^n or inside b^n c^n, so pumping cannot keep all three counts equal.

questions.q: Compared with the pumping lemma for regular languages, the CFL version pumps:
o: two substrings (v and x) instead of one
questions.e: The regular lemma pumps a single middle part y; the CFL lemma pumps two parts v and x simultaneously, reflecting the branching of derivation trees.

questions.q: The language LW = {ww | w ∈ {a,b}*} is:
questions.e: LW is not context-free; the proof uses z = a^n b^n a^n b^n and a case analysis showing every decomposition yields a word outside LW when pumped.

questions.q: Setting k = 0 in the CFL pumping lemma (pumping down) yields which word that must still be in L?
questions.e: With k = 0 the pumped parts v and x are deleted, giving uwy, which condition (iii) requires to be in L.

questions.q: For a CFL, the existence of the pumping number n is guaranteed provided the language is:
questions.e: The lemma states: if L is context-free, then such an n ≥ 1 exists; the property is derived from a CFG (e.g. in CNF) for L.

questions.q: In the proof that LW = {ww | w ∈ {a,b}*} is not context-free, the chosen word z is:
questions.e: The proof selects z = a^n b^n a^n b^n ∈ LW so that pumping within any single block breaks the required equality of the two halves.

questions.q: A context-sensitive grammar allows rules of which form?
o: β1 A β2 → β1 α β2 with α ≠ ε
questions.e: CSG rules have the form β1 A β2 → β1 α β2 (with α ≠ ε): the nonterminal A may be replaced by α only in the context of β1 and β2.

questions.q: Standard context-sensitive grammars (without the special start rule) cannot generate:
questions.e: Because every rule requires α ≠ ε (rules are non-contracting), a CSG cannot produce the empty word — unless one specially allows S → ε for the start symbol.

questions.q: The example grammar Gabc (with rules like S → abc | aABc, CB → BC, etc.) generates the language:
questions.e: Gabc generates {a^n b^n c^n | n ≥ 1}, a classic context-sensitive (but not context-free) language.

questions.q: The key non-contracting property of context-sensitive derivations is that whenever γ → δ:
questions.e: In a CSG every derivation step is non-contracting: |γ| ≤ |δ|, so sentential forms never shrink. This bounds the search and makes the word problem decidable.

questions.q: The word problem 'w ∈ L(G)?' for context-sensitive grammars is:
questions.e: It is decidable: because derivations are non-contracting, one can search backward from w over the finitely many sentential forms of length ≤ |w|, so the search terminates.

questions.q: The emptiness problem 'L(G) = ∅?' for context-sensitive grammars is:
questions.e: For CSGs the emptiness problem is undecidable, unlike the word problem which is decidable.

questions.q: The automaton model that exactly characterises the context-sensitive languages is the:
questions.e: A language is context-sensitive if and only if it is recognised by a linear bounded automaton — an NFA-like machine that moves both directions and may overwrite the tape, using space linear in the input.

questions.q: A general (unrestricted) grammar allows rules α → β where the left side α:
o: is any string over N∪Σ that is not purely terminal
questions.e: Type-0 (general) grammars permit α → β for α ∈ (N∪Σ)*\Σ* (α must contain a nonterminal) and any β; this is the most general grammar class.

questions.q: In the Chomsky hierarchy, which grammar type corresponds to context-free grammars?
questions.e: The Chomsky hierarchy numbers them: Type 0 general, Type 1 context-sensitive, Type 2 context-free, Type 3 right-linear (regular).

questions.q: In the Chomsky hierarchy, Type-3 grammars are the:
questions.e: Type 3 grammars are the right-linear grammars, generating exactly the regular languages.

questions.q: The automaton model corresponding to general (Type-0) grammars is the:
questions.e: General grammars can simulate any computation, and their matching automaton is the Turing machine — a universal computation model.

questions.q: For which grammar type is the word problem UNDECIDABLE?
questions.e: The word problem is decidable for Types 1, 2 and 3 but undecidable for Type-0 general grammars.

questions.q: According to the hierarchy's decidability table, the equivalence problem L(G1)=L(G2) is decidable only for which type?
questions.e: Equivalence is undecidable for Types 0, 1 and 2, and decidable only for Type-3 (regular) languages.

questions.q: What is the relationship between context-free and context-sensitive languages?
o: every context-free language is context-sensitive, and some CS languages are not context-free
questions.e: Every context-free language is context-sensitive, and there exist context-sensitive languages (e.g. {a^n b^n c^n}) that are not context-free — a proper inclusion.

questions.q: A linear bounded automaton is characterised as:
o: a restricted (nondeterministic) Turing machine whose tape is bounded by a linear function of the input length
questions.e: An LBA is a restricted NTM: it is essentially a Turing machine confined to a tape whose length is a linear function of the input size, unable to move past the input region.

questions.q: For which grammar types is the emptiness problem undecidable?
questions.e: Emptiness is undecidable for Type-0 (general) and Type-1 (context-sensitive) grammars, but decidable for Type-2 (CF) and Type-3 (regular).

questions.q: A (deterministic) Turing machine is defined as a tuple with how many components?
questions.e: A TM is the 7-tuple (Q, Σ, Γ, B, q0, q̄, δ): states, input alphabet, tape alphabet, blank symbol, initial state, final state, and transition function.

questions.q: In a Turing machine, the tape alphabet Γ and input alphabet Σ are related by:
o: Γ ⊃ Σ (tape alphabet strictly contains the input alphabet)
questions.e: The tape alphabet properly contains the input alphabet, Γ ⊃ Σ, since Γ must also include the blank symbol B (and possibly working symbols).

questions.q: The blank symbol B of a Turing machine satisfies:
questions.e: The blank B is a tape symbol that is not an input symbol: B ∈ Γ \ Σ.

questions.q: The transition function of a deterministic TM has the form:
questions.e: δ maps a (non-final) state and a scanned tape symbol to a new state, a symbol to write, and a head move: δ : (Q\{q̄}) × Γ → Q × Γ × {L, R, N}.

questions.q: The head-movement directions available to a Turing machine in one step are:
o: left, right, or no move (L, R, N)
questions.e: Each step moves the head one cell left (L), one cell right (R), or leaves it in place (N).

questions.q: At the start of a TM computation, the head is positioned:
o: at a fixed cell far to the left
over the first symbol of the input word
questions.e: Initially the input w is on the tape surrounded by blanks, the state is q0, and the head is over the first symbol of w.

questions.q: When a TM is used for a decision problem, it accepts the input exactly when it halts and:
o: the output word begins with a 1
questions.e: For decision problems the answer is read off as: accept if it terminates with the output beginning with 1, otherwise reject.

questions.q: A language L is called recursive (TM-decidable) if there is a TM that:
o: halts on all inputs and accepts w iff w ∈ L
questions.e: L is decidable/recursive iff some TM halts on every input and accepts exactly the words of L.

questions.q: A configuration of a Turing machine is written as a string αqβ, where:
o: α is the input and β the output
αβ is the tape content, q the state, and the head is over the first symbol of β
q is on the tape and α, β are states
questions.e: In configuration αqβ the tape holds αβ (surrounded by blanks), the current state is q, and the head scans the first symbol of β.

questions.q: A decision problem is modelled as a language by taking:
questions.e: For a decision function f : Σ* → {0,1}, the associated language is L = f⁻¹(1), the set of inputs whose answer is 'yes' (1).

questions.q: A problem with a unique output per input is naturally modelled as:
questions.e: When each input has one correct output, the problem is a function f : Σ* → Σ*; the general case (several feasible outputs) uses a relation.

questions.q: The running time of a Turing machine computation is defined as:
o: the number of state transitions until termination
the number of tape cells used
questions.e: Runtime is the number of state transitions (steps) performed until the machine halts.

questions.q: The memory (space) used by a Turing machine computation is:
o: the number of tape cells visited during the computation
questions.e: Space usage is measured by the number of distinct tape cells the head visits over the computation.

questions.q: A distinctive possibility of Turing-machine computation, absent in DFAs and PDAs on finite input, is that:
o: the computation may fail to terminate (loop forever)
questions.e: A TM may never reach its final state; in that case the computation does not terminate — non-termination is an inherent possibility.

questions.q: To compute the product of two binary numbers, a TM uses a separator symbol so that multiplication is the function:
questions.e: With the extended alphabet {0,1,#}, multiplication is f(bin(i1) # bin(i2)) = bin(i1 · i2); the # separates the two operands on the tape.

questions.q: A function f : Σ* → Σ* is called recursive (TM-computable) when:
o: there is a TM that computes f(x) from input x
questions.e: f is TM-computable/recursive iff some Turing machine, on input x, halts having produced the value f(x) on its tape.

questions.q: A nondeterministic Turing machine (NTM) differs from a deterministic one in that its transition δ is:
o: a relation δ ⊆ (Q\{q̄}) × Γ × Q × Γ × {L,R,N}
questions.e: For an NTM the transition is a relation, allowing several possible moves per (state, symbol) pair, whereas a DTM's δ is a function.

questions.q: The programming trick 'storage in the state' enlarges the state set to:
questions.e: To remember k tape symbols in the finite control, the state set is expanded by a factor |Γ|^k: Qnew = Q × Γ^k.

questions.q: The 'multi-track' trick represents k tracks per cell by extending the tape alphabet to:
questions.e: A k-track machine stores k symbols per cell by using k-dimensional vectors: Γnew = Γ ∪ Γ^k, with δ : Q × Γ^k → Q × Γ^k × {L,R,N}.

questions.q: For a k-tape Turing machine, the transition function has the form:
questions.e: A k-tape TM reads/writes on all k tapes at once: δ : (Q\{q̄}) × Γ^k → Q × Γ^k × {L,R,N}^k, with each tape having its own head move.

questions.q: In a multi-tape Turing machine, which tape serves as the input/output tape?
questions.e: Tape 1 is the input/output tape (as in the 1-tape TM); the remaining tapes 2,…,k start blank and serve as work tapes.

questions.q: Simulating a k-tape TM (time t(n)) by a single-tape TM incurs a time cost of:
questions.e: The standard simulation of a k-tape machine on one tape runs in time O(t²(n)) and space O(s(n)).

questions.q: The single-tape simulation of a k-tape TM uses how many tracks?
questions.e: It uses 2k tracks: the odd tracks hold the k tape contents and the even tracks mark the k head positions with the symbol #.

questions.q: The universal Turing machine U receives its input in the form:
o: ⟨M⟩w — the encoding of a machine M followed by a word w
questions.e: U is programmable: its input is ⟨M⟩w, the Gödel number of a TM M concatenated with an arbitrary word w, and U simulates M on w.

questions.q: The encoding ⟨M⟩ of a Turing machine used by the universal TM is called its:
questions.e: The encoding of M is its Gödel number ⟨M⟩, a binary string that acts as the 'program' fed to the universal machine.

questions.q: Gödel numbers are required to be prefix-free, which is enforced by the convention that every code:
o: begins and ends with 111, and 111 does not otherwise occur inside
questions.e: Prefix-freeness is achieved by making every Gödel number start and end with 111 while forbidding the substring 111 anywhere in between.

questions.q: A single transition δ(qi, Xj) = (qk, Xl, Dm) is encoded (in the Gödel-number scheme) as the binary string:
o: i j k l m in binary
questions.e: Each transition is coded in unary-with-separators as 0^i 1 0^j 1 0^k 1 0^l 1 0^m, listing the indices of the state, read symbol, next state, written symbol and move.

questions.q: In the Gödel-numbering convention, the tape symbols are numbered X1, X2, X3 standing for:
questions.e: The tape alphabet is numbered X1 = 0, X2 = 1, X3 = B (blank).

questions.q: In the Gödel-numbering convention, the head moves D1, D2, D3 stand for:
questions.e: The moves are numbered D1 = L, D2 = N, D3 = R.

questions.q: In the standardized form of TMs used for Gödel numbering, which state is the halting (stopping) state?
questions.e: The convention fixes q1 as the initial state and q2 as the halting state.

questions.q: When the universal TM is implemented as a 3-band machine, band 2 and band 3 hold, respectively:
o: the Gödel number of M, and the current state of M
questions.e: Band 1 simulates M's tape, band 2 stores the Gödel number ⟨M⟩, and band 3 records M's current state.

questions.q: The Church–Turing thesis asserts that Turing-machine power coincides with which other models?
o: λ-calculus, Post's canonical systems, and μ-recursive functions
questions.e: Turing computability is equivalent to Church's λ-calculus, Post's canonical systems, and Kleene's μ-recursive functions — the basis of the Church–Turing thesis (1930s).

questions.q: A linear bounded automaton marks the ends of its working region with the endmarker symbols:
o: $ on the left and # on the right
# on the left and $ on the right
questions.e: The LBA input is delimited as $ a1…an #, with $ the left endmarker and # the right endmarker; the head may not move past them.

questions.q: For an LBA with q states, tape length n and tape-alphabet size g, the number of distinct configurations is:
questions.e: Because the tape is bounded, the number of distinct configurations is q · n · g^n, which is finite — this is what makes the LBA acceptance analysis terminate.
